source_text: Similiter inpudicitiam omnem amoliri iubemur. hoc igitur modo etiam a theatro separamur, quod est priuatum consistorium inpudicitiae, ubi nihil probatur quam quod alibi non probatur. ita summa gratia eius de spurcitia plurimum concinnata est, quam Atellanus gesticulatur, quam mimus etiam per muliebres res repraesentat, sensum sexus et pudoris exterminans, ut facilius domi quam in scaena erubescant, quam denique pantomimus a pueritia patitur ex corpore, ut artifex esse possit. ipsa etiam prostibula, publicae libidinis hostiae, in scaena proferuntur, plus miserae in praesentia feminarum, quibus solis latebant, perque omnis aetatis, omnis dignitatis ora transducuntur; locus, stipes, elogium, etiam quibus opus non est, praedicatur, etiam (taceo de reliquis) [etiam] quae in tenebris et in speluncis suis delitescere decebat, ne diem contaminarent. erubescat senatus, erubescant ordines omnes; ipsae illae pudoris sui interemptrices de gestibus suis ad lucem et populum expauescentes semel anno erubescant. quodsi nobis omnis impudicitia exsecranda est, cur liceat audire quod loqui non licet, cum etiam scurrilitatem et omne uanum uer-. bum iudicatum a deo sciamus? cur aeque liceat uidere - quae facere flagitium est? cur quae ore prolata communicant hominem, ea per aures et oculos admissa non uideantur hominem communicare, cum spiritui appareant aures et oculi nec possit mundus praestari cuius apparitores inquinantur? habes igitur et theatri interdictionem de interdictione impudicitiae. si et doctrinam saecularis litteraturae ut stultitiae apud deum deputatam aspernamur, satis praescribitur nobis et de illis speciebus spectaculorum, quae saeculari litteratura lusoriam uel agonisticam scaenam dispungunt. quodsi sunt tragoediae et comoediae scelerum et libidinum actrices cruentae et lasciuae, impiae et prodigae, nullius rei aut atrocis aut uilis commemoratio melior est: quod in facto reicitur, etiam in dicto non est recipiendum.
thought_title: The theater is condemned as a school of impurity
orientation: Tertullian is arguing that since Scripture forbids impurity, Christians are thereby separated from the theater, which is its private council-chamber.
pass_a_gloss: In like manner we are commanded to put away all impurity. In this way therefore we are also separated from the theater, which is the private council-chamber of impurity, where nothing is approved except what is not approved elsewhere. So its highest charm is composed very much of filth, which the Atellanus actor gestures, which the mime even represents through female roles, destroying the sense of sex and of modesty, so that they blush more easily at home than on the stage, which finally the pantomime suffers from boyhood in his body, so that he may be able to be an artist. Even the prostitutes themselves, victims of public lust, are brought forward on the stage, more wretched in the presence of women, from whom alone they used to hide, and they are led past the faces of every age, of every rank; their place, their fee, their notice, even things for which there is no need, are proclaimed, even (I am silent about the rest) things which ought to hide in darkness and in their caves, lest they pollute the day. Let the senate blush, let all the orders blush; let those very murderesses of their own modesty, shuddering at the light and the people because of their gestures, blush once a year. But if all impurity is to be abominated by us, why should it be permitted to hear what it is not permitted to speak, since we know that even scurrility and every vain word has been judged by God? Why should it equally be permitted to see what it is a disgrace to do? Why should the things which, brought forth by the mouth, defile a man, not seem to defile a man when admitted through the ears and eyes, since the ears and eyes appear to the spirit, and he cannot be rendered clean whose attendants are defiled? You have therefore also the prohibition of the theater from the prohibition of impurity. If we also spurn the teaching of secular literature as reckoned foolishness with God, enough is prescribed for us also concerning those kinds of shows, which secular literature marks out as the playful or athletic stage. But if tragedies and comedies are bloody and wanton, impious and prodigal actresses of crimes and lusts, no mention of anything either atrocious or vile is better: what is rejected in deed must not be received even in word.

choices.why: Consistorium is a formal term for an imperial council chamber; 'private' preserves priuatum and the irony that impurity holds its own court in the theater.

choices.english: destroying the sense of sex and of modesty
choices.why: Exterminans means driving out or abolishing; 'sense of sex' keeps the literal sensum sexus, meaning the awareness of one's own sex and its proper modesty.
rejected: banishing the sense of sex and shame
destroying the feeling of gender and modesty

choices.why: Hostiae are sacrificial victims; the metaphor is that prostitutes are offered up to public lust, so 'victims' preserves the sacrificial force.

choices.english: those very murderesses of their own modesty
choices.why: Interemptrix is a feminine agent noun meaning murderer or destroyer; 'murderesses' keeps the strong, violent image Tertullian uses.
rejected: those very destroyers of their own modesty
those very killers of their own shame

choices.why: Apparitores are official attendants or servants of a magistrate; the ears and eyes are pictured as the spirit's attendants, so 'attendants' preserves the official metaphor.
Dispungo means to mark off or assign; secular literature assigns or marks out the playful and athletic stage, so 'marks out' keeps the sense of designation.

pass_b_english: In the same way, we are commanded to put away all impurity. This is how we are separated from the theater as well. The theater is impurity's own council chamber, where nothing is approved except what is not approved anywhere else. Its highest charm is built up entirely from filth. Atellanus acts out that filth with gestures. The mime represents it even through women's roles, destroying the sense of sex and of modesty, so that people blush more easily at home than on stage. The pantomime suffers that filth in his body from boyhood, so that he can become an artist. Even the prostitutes themselves, the victims of public lust, are brought out on stage. They are more wretched in the presence of women, from whom alone they used to hide. They are paraded before the faces of every age and every rank. Their location, their price, their notice are proclaimed even to those who have no need of them. Even what should have hidden in darkness and in their own caves, to keep from contaminating the daylight, is proclaimed. I say nothing of the rest. Let the senate blush. Let all the orders blush. Let those very destroyers of their own modesty, terrified by their own gestures before the light and the people, blush once a year.

But if all impurity is to be abominated by us, why should it be lawful to hear what it is not lawful to speak? We know that even scurrility and every idle word is judged by God. Why should it be equally lawful to see what it is a crime to do? Why should the things that defile a person when brought out through the mouth not seem to defile a person when admitted through the ears and eyes? The ears and eyes are the spirit's attendants, and a person cannot be kept clean whose attendants are polluted. You have, then, the prohibition of the theater from the prohibition of impurity.

If we also reject the teaching of secular literature as counted foolishness before God, enough is prescribed for us concerning those kinds of shows that secular literature marks out as the playful or athletic stage. But if tragedies and comedies are bloody and wanton actresses of crimes and lusts, impious and extravagant, no remembrance of anything atrocious or vile is better. What is rejected in deed must not be received even in word.

last_rejected.quote: those very murderesses of their own modesty, terrified by their own gestures
last_rejected.source_quote: ipsae illae pudoris sui interemptrices de gestibus suis
last_rejected.why: Latin says they are 'interemptrices' (those who interpose themselves in their own modesty), not murderesses; agency and sense are wrong.
last_rejected.fix: those who interpose themselves in their own modesty, terrified by their own gestures
last_rejected.ruling: interemptrices derives from interimo 'to destroy/kill'; 'murderesses of modesty' is valid. de gestibus suis = 'by their gestures,' not 'terrified by.'

polish.changed: Broke long sentences into clearer units, made the subject of each clause explicit, and clarified the sequence of Tertullian's argument about impurity, the theater, and secular literature.

notes.why: Distinction between types of stage is unclear; reader may not know what 'playful' stage means.

problems.quote: Let those very murderesses of their own modesty
problems.why: 'Murderesses' for women who kill their modesty? Strong but odd.

edits.old: Let those very murderesses of their own modesty
edits.new: Let those very destroyers of their own modesty

fixed: Changed 'murderesses' to 'destroyers' for 'interemptrices' (from 'interimo', to destroy/do away with), which is the more accurate rendering; 'murderesses' overstates the metaphor.
